url_citation.content:
In Brief | In Brief Review
Triggered focus

Some radical – and some scientific – claims about social status

By Paul Seabright
The TLS front page from the issue dated Triggered focus. Issue number
© Ella Baron
November 12, 2021
Read this issue

In this review

THE STATUS GAME
On social position and how we use it 416pp. William Collins. £20.
Will Storr
All blurb-writers exaggerate, but even by these standards the following claim is a whopper: “For centuries, philosophers and scholars have described human behaviour in terms of sex, power and money … bestselling author Will Storr radically turns this thinking on its head by arguing that it is our irrepressible craving for status that ultimately defines who we are”. How to begin to unpack such exaggeration? Perhaps by noting that of the hundreds of researchers who for decades have studied the human desire for status, quite a few are cited here in support. (I almost wrote “distinguished researchers”, but that would be to fall into Storr’s trap of thinking their status matters more than their logic and evidence.)
There are indeed radical claims in this book, and scientifically accurate ones, but the two rarely overlap. Take the (radical) claim that “everyone alive today is still coded to play hunter gatherer games. These rules are stored in our DNA”. DNA matters for behaviour, certainly.

...

The Status Game cites many studies but with little sense of which are reliable, which controversial and which speculative.

url_citation.title: The Status Game with Will Storr - Intelligence Squared
url_citation.content:
This is just one of the fascinating findings that bestselling writer Will Storr shares when he came to Intelligence Squared in September 2021 to discuss the themes of his new book The Status Game. Storr argued that it is our irrepressible craving for status that ultimately defines who we are. As he puts it, ‘If you want to rule the world, save the world, buy the world or fuck the world, the best thing to pursue is status.’ And research shows that without sufficient status, we suffer more illness and live shorter lives.
Storr identified what he calls two ‘prestige games’ that humans play to acquire status: success games and virtue games. Success games are about having a fast car or winning a promotion. In the more complex virtue games, people compete for prestige through demonstrations of moral goodness, believing that they are motivated not by a desire for status, but by their superior goodness. This, Storr argued, can lead to pressure to hold ‘correct’ beliefs in order to maintain one’s social status.
Drawing from anthropology, sociology, and psychology, Storr examined the unconscious obsession that drives the best and worst of us: our innovations, our arts and our civilisation as well

# The Status Game

by Will Storr · 2021

A journalist argues that the drive for status, not happiness or money, is the hidden engine behind almost all human behavior, and that we play three distinct status games (dominance, virtue, and success) often without realizing which one we're in.

**Worth reading?** Storr's thesis is that status, not wealth or pleasure, is the currency human psychology is actually optimizing for, and he identifies three distinct games people play for it:

...

It's rigorously reported, drawing on psychology, history, and Storr's own interviews, and lands as one of the more genuinely explanatory books about tribalism and moral panic published in recent years.
